nameStory: The Common Moon Jelly gets its dreamy name from its translucent, circular bell that looks remarkably like a glowing full moon floating through the water. When light filters through its ghostly pale body, it creates an ethereal, moon-like appearance that has captivated observers for centuries. The 'jelly' part comes from its soft, gelatinous texture that feels like firm Jell-O when touched.
description: The Common Moon Jelly is a translucent, umbrella-shaped jellyfish that drifts gracefully through New England's coastal waters. Its bell-shaped body is nearly transparent with a subtle bluish or pinkish tint, and you can often see four distinctive horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs through its clear flesh. These gentle jellies typically measure 4-12 inches across their bell. Unlike some of their more dangerous cousins, moon jellies have only a mild sting that most people barely notice.

idTips.label: Four-leaf clover pattern
idTips.description: Look through the transparent bell for four distinctive horseshoe or kidney-shaped structures that resemble a four-leaf clover - these are the reproductive organs and are the moon jelly's signature feature

idTips.label: Transparent bell
idTips.description: The dome-shaped body is crystal clear to slightly milky white, often with a faint bluish or pinkish tinge that shimmers in sunlight

idTips.label: Short, frilly tentacles
idTips.description: Around the bell's edge, numerous short, delicate tentacles create a lacy fringe that feels slightly sticky to the touch but produces only a mild tingle

idTips.label: Gentle pulsing motion
idTips.description: Swims with slow, rhythmic contractions of its bell, creating a hypnotic pumping motion as it propels itself through the water

idTips.label: Jelly-like texture
idTips.description: When washed up on shore, feels like firm gelatin - bouncy and slippery but holds its shape when gently poked

habitat: Common Moon Jellies inhabit New England's coastal waters from shallow bays and harbors to deeper offshore areas. They're especially common in protected waters like estuaries and salt marshes where the water is calmer, and you'll often spot them from piers, beaches, or boats during summer months. After storms, you might find their clear, dome-shaped bodies washed up on sandy beaches from Maine to Connecticut.

seasonality.spring: Moon jellies begin appearing in warmer coastal waters as temperatures rise, often first spotted in protected bays and harbors where the water warms earliest.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for moon jelly sightings - they're abundant in shallow coastal waters and frequently visible from beaches, docks, and boats, often forming loose groups or blooms.
seasonality.fall: Still present in warmer waters but numbers decline as temperatures drop, with occasional specimens washing ashore after autumn storms.
seasonality.winter: Largely absent from New England waters, having moved to deeper, warmer areas or died off, leaving only tiny polyps attached to underwater surfaces.

funFact: Moon jellies are about 95% water and have no brain, blood, or heart, yet they've survived for over 500 million years - making them older than dinosaurs and even trees, and proving that sometimes the simplest designs are the most successful!
confusionNotes: Moon jellies are sometimes confused with other clear jellies, but remember the "four-leaf clover" - those four horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs visible through the bell are unique to moon jellies. If you can't see this distinctive pattern, you're likely looking at a different species.
contextualKnowledge: The Common Moon Jelly was once thought to be found worldwide, but scientists recently discovered that what we called "one species" was actually at least 28 different species! The true Common Moon Jelly is only found in the North Atlantic, making our New England populations some of the only places to see the "real" moon jelly.
compareHints: The Common Moon Jelly differs from its close relatives by its specific four-horseshoe pattern and North Atlantic location. The Southern Moon Jelly has a slightly different reproductive organ arrangement, while the Greater Moon Jelly grows much larger. In New England waters, if you see the classic four-leaf clover pattern in a moderately-sized clear jelly, you're almost certainly looking at the Common Moon Jelly.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Southern Moon Jellies are virtually indistinguishable from Common Moon Jellies by appearance alone - both share the telltale four horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs and crystal-clear bell.
Greater Moon Jellies are typically larger than Common Moon Jellies, though their size ranges overlap significantly.
